answers.java_tx_design: The clearest case was in our reservation-ledger service, the system that holds a booking in a pending state while we call three or four hotel-partner APIs to confirm the room is still available. For about a year we wrapped the whole hold-and-confirm flow in one Spring @Transactional method, so the DB transaction stayed open across those outbound calls. When a partner's API got slow -- one incident had their p99 hit 4 seconds -- the transaction held row locks on the booking row for the same 4 seconds, and during a Friday evening spike we had over 200 threads queued waiting on the same lock. I split it: the hold commits immediately in its own short transaction with status PENDING_CONFIRM, the partner calls happen with no open transaction, and a second short transaction flips the status to CONFIRMED or releases the hold. Lock hold time dropped from seconds to single-digit milliseconds. The failure I hadn't anticipated: a crash between the two transactions left holds stuck in PENDING_CONFIRM, which is why we added a 15-minute sweep job to release them.
answers.java_ops: Same service, different problem: HikariCP connection pool exhaustion. During a regional sale, every booking request also fired a synchronous read to check loyalty-tier discounts, and those reads borrowed from the same 30-connection pool as the booking writes. Pool wait time, which we graph in Grafana, went from under 5ms to over 1200ms at p99, and requests started timing out at 3 seconds. I pulled the connection-acquisition histogram, confirmed it wasn't a DB-side slowdown, and split the loyalty read onto its own pool of 10 connections instead of sharing the write pool. I also dropped the write pool's maximumPoolSize from 30 to 20 and raised headroom on the database side, since 30 was oversubscribing a database that maxed out at 100 total connections across four service instances. Pool wait dropped to under 10ms at p99 and we stopped seeing timeouts during the next two sales events.
answers.rust_readiness: I don't have production Rust experience, so I'll be straight about that. What I've done is work through the official book and rewrite a small internal tool -- a settlement-total recalculator that reads our nightly CSV export and cross-checks it against the ledger -- twice, once in Java and once in Rust, to force myself to hit ownership and borrowing for real rather than just reading about them. My plan for getting to production-ready: a first month on more of that kind of side-by-side rewrite for low-stakes, batch-oriented code, then a small async worker using tokio over the following two months, before I'd trust myself to own a service boundary. On where I'd start in a system like the one I described: I would not touch the transactional booking core early. I'd pick something stateless and easy to verify by comparing outputs, like fee calculation, and run it in parallel with the Java version before cutting over.
answers.rust_boundary: If I were moving part of a ledger write path, I would not start with the write path itself. I'd start by profiling which sub-computation is hottest and least stateful -- in my current system that's the fee calculation step, pure math over a booking and a rate table, no DB writes of its own. I'd put it behind a small gRPC interface the Java service calls, keep the Java version running in parallel, and log both results without acting on the Rust one for a few weeks. What I'd watch before and after: p99 latency of that call, error rate, and a daily count of mismatches between the two outputs. Only once mismatches were at zero for a sustained period would I let the Rust result become authoritative and eventually remove the Java path. I don't have a past example of cutting this exact boundary, so I want to be honest that this is a plan, not something I've already proven.
answers.money_correctness: In the reservation-ledger service, every payment attempt carries an idempotency key made from booking_id plus a hash of the attempt payload, stored in an idempotency_keys table with a 24-hour TTL and a unique constraint. When the gateway retries a webhook, or our own retry logic fires after a timeout, we look up the key first and return the stored result instead of charging again. This broke once, in November two years ago: a gateway-side retry storm resent the same webhook with a slightly different payload hash 340 times over about six hours, because a partner's system regenerated a signature field on resend, so our hash-based key treated each resend as new. We caught it from a spike in our daily reconciliation job, which flagged $18,400 in holds with no matching confirmed booking. We fixed it by keying on booking_id plus gateway transaction ID instead of a payload hash, and corrected the 340 holds with reversing entries rather than deleting them, so the ledger kept a full record of what happened.
answers.incident_response: Separate incident, same service, about a year later: a race condition let two concurrent requests both read a room as available before either had written its hold, so we double-booked 12 rooms over one weekend. I got paged at 2:14 a.m. by an alert on booking-conflict rate, had the query isolating the affected reservations by 2:50, and had a fix deployed -- an application-level lock keyed on room and date, held for the duration of the hold check -- by 6:10 a.m. I told the on-call lead and our hotel-partner ops contact by 3 a.m., before the fix was even out, because guests needed to be rebooked or compensated. The postmortem's main change was that lock, plus a monitor on booking-conflict rate with a much lower threshold; we've had zero repeats of that specific race in the two years since. My mistake in the initial response was assuming it was a partner-side data issue for the first 20 minutes, which cost time I'd have saved by checking our own locking first.
answers.process_skipping: During the double-booking incident I just described, someone on the call suggested pushing the lock fix straight to production without the usual second reviewer, since it was 3 a.m. and guests were actively being double-booked. What we actually did: post in the incident channel that we were skipping full review, get one other engineer to eyeball the diff over a five-minute call instead of the normal async review, and deploy with that recorded in the incident log. Once things were stable, we did a full retroactive review the next morning and found a small issue with the lock's timeout value, which we then fixed properly. My bar for skipping the normal procedure: real, active harm happening right now, someone else's eyes on the change even if abbreviated, and a record of what was skipped and why, followed by catching up on the full process once the fire is out. I've turned down skipping it a few times when the pressure was really about a deadline, not actual harm.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: On sharing a mistake: about three years ago I misconfigured a feature-flag rollout, wrote 50 instead of 5, and put a broken discount-calculation path in front of ten times more traffic than intended. I noticed the error-rate graph moving within about ten minutes, and before I'd even fully diagnosed it I posted in our team channel that I thought I'd caused it and was rolling the flag back, rather than waiting until I was sure. It turned out to be exactly that. On-call: I've been on our rotation for about four years, one week in five, averaging two to three pages a month, mostly connection-pool or partner-timeout alerts. I also mentor two junior engineers, pairing with each roughly weekly, and I onboarded both of them into on-call once they'd shadowed a few rotations. I've never thought of on-call or answering a junior's questions as separate from my actual job; it's the same job.
answers.evidence_decision: About two years ago the team wanted to move our booking-hold logic to a distributed lock service, arguing it would scale better than the row-level locking I'd designed. I disagreed and pulled six weeks of production latency data showing our current approach held locks for under 10ms at p99, well under any pain point, and benchmarked in staging that the distributed lock service would add 15 to 20ms of network overhead per hold. The team looked at the numbers and decided to keep row-level locking for now, revisiting only if hold volume grew past a threshold we set together. I didn't relitigate it afterward, and when hold volume did grow eighteen months later, I was the one who flagged that we were approaching the agreed threshold, and we opened the distributed-lock work as a planned project rather than me building it on the side first to prove a point.
answers.own_contribution: In the fee-calculation migration I described for Rust, the shadow-mode boundary decision is entirely my own plan, not yet executed, so I don't want to overstate it as team consensus -- it's untested judgment I'm describing honestly. For something that did happen: in the idempotency-key incident, deciding to re-key on booking_id plus gateway transaction ID instead of a payload hash was my call after I traced the 340 mismatched holds myself in the reconciliation logs; the team's part was reviewing and approving the change, and another engineer built the backfill script from my specification. So the split was: I found the root cause and designed the fix, someone else implemented the backfill tooling, and the team approved deploying it during a change freeze.
answers.java_recovery: The 340-hold incident I mentioned is also my clearest data-recovery example. Once we knew the cause, I wrote a query to scope every idempotency_keys row created in that six-hour window with a gateway transaction ID that also appeared under a different key, which gave me the 340 affected holds. For each one I confirmed against the gateway's own transaction log whether the booking had actually been charged twice before deciding on a fix, since I didn't want to assume every flagged row was a real duplicate. 12 of the 340 turned out to be legitimate retries with no double charge, so I only corrected 328. I fixed those with a reversing ledger entry dated to the discovery time rather than editing the original entry, then ran the nightly reconciliation job manually against just those 328 booking IDs to confirm the balances matched the gateway's records afterward, which they did on the first pass.
answers.java_perf_change: We had a checkout endpoint sitting at p99 of 640ms against an SLA target of 300ms. I profiled it with async-profiler and found a synchronous call to a tax-rate service for every line item in a booking, sometimes six or seven calls per request, each averaging 60-80ms. My first attempt was a short-lived in-memory cache per request, which helped almost nothing, 640ms to 600ms, because most requests had unique line-item combinations. What actually worked was batching all the line items in one request into a single call to the tax service, using a batch endpoint we weren't yet calling. That took p99 down to 210ms. I made the batching optional behind a flag so we could roll it back instantly, which we didn't end up needing, and kept the per-item path as a fallback for the one caller that couldn't batch yet.
answers.rust_hands_on: The settlement-recalculator side project is the only real Rust I've written, so I'll describe that honestly rather than dress it up. I got stuck holding a running total in a struct while iterating over borrowed references to the day's transactions and also wanting to push corrections into a separate Vec as I found them; the borrow checker rejected it because I was holding an immutable borrow of the transaction list while trying to mutably borrow my corrections vector inside the same loop. I fixed it by collecting correction candidates into an intermediate Vec of indices first, ending that borrow, then doing the mutation in a second pass. It's a small fix, but it's the first time ownership stopped feeling like an abstract rule and started feeling like something I could reason about directly.
answers.rust_when_not: I'd hold back from moving anything with high change frequency and low team familiarity, which for us right now means most of the booking-hold and payment-confirmation core -- the part I described earlier that's had two real incidents and gets touched almost every sprint. I did once talk myself out of proposing a Rust rewrite of our webhook-ingestion layer, which handles gateway callbacks, because when I measured it, its p99 was 40ms against a 200ms SLA -- not a performance problem, just a language I found more appealing to write in. I decided the honest reason I wanted to touch it was preference, not need, so I didn't bring it to the team as a project. My criteria: is there a measured problem, is the surface area stable enough to verify a rewrite is equivalent, and would the team maintaining it going forward actually want to own it in the new language.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: During a monthly reconciliation about eighteen months ago, our totals were off by $4,800 across roughly 2,200 bookings, small enough per-booking to go unnoticed -- about $2.18 average -- but consistent enough that I didn't believe it was random rounding. I traced it to currency conversion: we converted the room rate to the guest's currency at booking time and again at settlement time using whatever rate that day happened to have, and a five-day gap between booking and settlement during a period of rate volatility produced the drift. I corrected the affected bookings with adjusting entries at the settlement-time rate, dated to when I made the correction rather than backdated. Going forward we locked the conversion rate at booking time and carried it through to settlement instead of reconverting, which is the actual fix; my first guess, before I found this, was a partner refund-timing issue, which turned out to be unrelated.
answers.prod_data_verification: Yes, more than once. The clearest case was after the double-booking incident, when I wanted to confirm the new room-and-date lock actually prevented the race under real concurrent load, and production was the only place with that traffic pattern. Instead of testing against real bookings, I took a masked snapshot of a slow week's traffic -- same request shapes and timing, guest names and payment details replaced -- and replayed it against a staging environment sized to match production concurrency. When that's not possible, like verifying a reconciliation fix against live settlement data, I've used read-only shadow queries that compute a result without writing anything, and compared that to the real ledger rather than editing anything live. I did once check one live balance directly during the 340-hold incident, to confirm my hypothesis before writing the correction script, and I posted in the incident channel exactly which booking ID I was looking at and why before I ran the query.
